claim: cAMP-PKA-CREB signaling is a pattern recognition receptor (PRR)-independent mechanism that regulates conventional type-2 Dendritic Cells (cDC2s) in mice.
source: Here we show that cAMP-PKA-CREB signaling (a pattern recognition receptor [PRR]-independent mechanism) regulates conventional type-2 Dendritic Cells (cDC2s) in mice and reprograms their Th17-inducing properties via repression of IRF4 and KLF4, transcription factors essential for cDC2-mediated Th2 induction.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding as a main result of the study.

claim: cAMP-PKA-CREB signaling reprograms cDC2s' Th17-inducing properties via repression of IRF4 and KLF4.

evidence: The abstract presents this as a key mechanistic finding supported by experimental data.

claim: 50% of IRF4 binding sites had ETS:IRF motifs similar to proposed EICEs.
source: We investigated the known TF motifs bound by IRF4 and found that they fell into three categories: 50% of the sites had ETS:IRF motifs similar to proposed EICEs (Brass et al., 1996; Ochiai et al., 2013), 24% had duplicated IRF motifs similar to ISREs (Bovolenta et al., 1994; Ochiai et al., 2013), and 23% had bZIP motifs similar to AICEs (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: 106 super enhancers with multiple IRF4 binding sites were identified.
source: Using the Young lab criteria, we found evidence for 106 super enhancers with multiple IRF4 binding sites (Supplementary file 1: containing Supplementary Table 16) (Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text based on ChIPseq analysis using established criteria.

claim: One super enhancer was located in the Il6 locus and had multiple binding sites for IRF4, BATF and PU.1.
source: Inspection of these super enhancers revealed that one was located in the Il6 locus and had multiple binding sites for IRF4, BATF and PU.1; these peaks corresponded to EICEs, AICEs and ISREs identified in the motif analysis (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Intranasal transfer of HDM-pulsed, CPT-treated WT cDC2s increased the production of IL-17A in the lung and airway of WT recipient mice.
source: Intranasal (i.n.) transfer of HDM-pulsed, CPT-treated or curdlan-treated WT cDC2s followed by HDM i.n challenge increased the production of IL-17A in the lung and airway of WT recipient mice (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Intranasal transfer of HDM-pulsed, curdlan-treated WT cDC2s increased the production of IL-17A in the lung and airway of WT recipient mice.
source: Intranasal (i.n.) transfer of HDM-pulsed, CPT-treated or curdlan-treated WT cDC2s followed by HDM i.n challenge increased the production of IL-17A in the lung and airway of WT recipient mice (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: An increased number of neutrophils was detected in the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid in the CPT- or curdlan-treated cDC2 groups.
source: We detected an increased number of neutrophils in the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid (Figure 6D–G) and expression of Cxcl2 and Cxcl3, whose expression accompanied neutrophilic infiltration in the CPT- or curdlan-treated cDC2 groups (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6D–G.

claim: Expression of Cxcl2 and Cxcl3 accompanied neutrophilic infiltration in the CPT- or curdlan-treated cDC2 groups.
source: We detected an increased number of neutrophils in the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid (Figure 6D–G) and expression of Cxcl2 and Cxcl3, whose expression accompanied neutrophilic infiltration in the CPT- or curdlan-treated cDC2 groups (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Expression of eosinophilic infiltration-related genes, Cd24a and Dpp4, was decreased in the CPT- or curdlan-treated cDC2 groups.
source: Expression of eosinophilic infiltration-related genes, Cd24a and Dpp4, was decreased in those groups (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: CPT- or curdlan-treated WT cDC2s transferred to WT recipient mice had increased airway resistance.
source: CPT- or curdlan-treated WT cDC2s transferred to WT recipient mice also had increased airway resistance (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) are germline-encoded proteins expressed primarily on innate immune cells.
source: Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) are germline-encoded proteins expressed primarily on innate immune cells that recognize conserved microbe- or pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), and damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMPs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: PRRs recognize conserved microbe- or pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), and damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMPs).
source: Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) are germline-encoded proteins expressed primarily on innate immune cells that recognize conserved microbe- or pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), and damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMPs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Triggering of PRRs results in the maturation of DCs and their subsequent activation-acquired properties to elicit and shape CD8+ T cells and CD4+ Th cells responses.
source: The main paradigm of immune activation posits that triggering of PRRs results in the maturation of DCs and their subsequent activation-acquired properties to elicit and shape CD8+ T cells and CD4+ Th cells responses (Hansen et al., 2011; Palm and Medzhitov, 2009; Takeuchi and Akira, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The splenic cDC1 subpopulation promotes CD4+ Th1 and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells (CTL) responses.
source: For example, the splenic cDC1 subpopulation, which promotes CD4+ Th1 and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells (CTL) responses, requires the TFs interferon regulatory factor 8 (IRF8) and basic leucine-zipper ATF-like transcription factor 3 (BATF3), whereas splenic cDC2s, which promote Th2 and Th17 responses, require IRF4 (Gao et al., 2013; Hambleton et al., 2011; Vander Lugt et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2013) and Kruppel-like factor 4 (KLF4) (Tussiwand et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The splenic cDC1 subpopulation requires the TFs interferon regulatory factor 8 (IRF8) and basic leucine-zipper ATF-like transcription factor 3 (BATF3).

claim: The cDC2s lineage has been divided into Th2-inducing (IRF4+/KLF4+), and Th17-inducing (IRF4+/NOTCH2+) subpopulations.
source: The cDC2s lineage has been further divided into Th2-inducing (IRF4+/KLF4+), and Th17-inducing (IRF4+/NOTCH2+) subpopulations (Bedoui and Heath, 2015; Tussiwand et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: IRF4 is induced as an immediate early gene by antigen receptors.
source: Induced as an immediate early gene by antigen receptors, IRF4's expression scales with the intensity of receptor signaling, thus linking the quality of antigen receptor signaling with B and T cell fate output (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2017; Man et al., 2013; Matsuyama et al., 1995; Nayar et al., 2014; Ochiai et al., 2013; Sciammas et al., 2006; Yao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: IRF4's expression scales with the intensity of receptor signaling.
source: Induced as an immediate early gene by antigen receptors, IRF4's expression scales with the intensity of receptor signaling, thus linking the quality of antigen receptor signaling with B and T cell fate output (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2017; Man et al., 2013; Matsuyama et al., 1995; Nayar et al., 2014; Ochiai et al., 2013; Sciammas et al., 2006; Yao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Expression of IRF4 is not induced by either Type I or Type II interferon.
source: In contrast to other members of the IRF family, expression of IRF4 is not induced by either Type I or Type II interferon (Matsuyama et al., 1995) but rather by different modes of NF-kB signaling induced by the antigen receptors, TLR, and TNF receptor systems (Shaffer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Expression of IRF4 is induced by different modes of NF-kB signaling induced by the antigen receptors, TLR, and TNF receptor systems.
source: In contrast to other members of the IRF family, expression of IRF4 is not induced by either Type I or Type II interferon (Matsuyama et al., 1995) but rather by different modes of NF-kB signaling induced by the antigen receptors, TLR, and TNF receptor systems (Shaffer et al., 2009).

claim: Low levels of cAMP in cDCs promote Th2 differentiation.
source: We have found that low levels of cAMP in cDCs promote Th2 differentiation (Lee et al., 2015) and high levels promote induction of Th17 (Datta et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors with supporting citations.

claim: High levels of cAMP in cDCs promote induction of Th17.
source: We have found that low levels of cAMP in cDCs promote Th2 differentiation (Lee et al., 2015) and high levels promote induction of Th17 (Datta et al., 2010).

claim: Curdlan is a linear polymer of β (1,3)-glucan derived from soil bacteria.
source: Curdlan is a linear polymer of β (1,3)-glucan derived from soil bacteria and the ligand of the PRR Dectin-1 (Yoshitomi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Curdlan is the ligand of the PRR Dectin-1.
source: Curdlan is a linear polymer of β (1,3)-glucan derived from soil bacteria and the ligand of the PRR Dectin-1 (Yoshitomi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Signaling by Dectin-1 involves recruitment of Syk to the Dectin-1 intracellular tail, followed by activation of MAPK, NF-κB and NFAT.
source: Signaling by Dectin-1 is independent of cAMP and involves recruitment of Syk to the Dectin-1 intracellular tail, followed by activation of MAPK, NF-κB and NFAT (Gross et al., 2006) and induction of IL-23, which promotes Th17 differentiation (LeibundGut-Landmann et al., 2007; Rogers et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Dectin-1 signaling induces IL-23, which promotes Th17 differentiation.
source: Signaling by Dectin-1 is independent of cAMP and involves recruitment of Syk to the Dectin-1 intracellular tail, followed by activation of MAPK, NF-κB and NFAT (Gross et al., 2006) and induction of IL-23, which promotes Th17 differentiation (LeibundGut-Landmann et al., 2007; Rogers et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: cDC2 plasticity is not accompanied by gross changes in chromatin structure.
source: We observed no significant differences (after multiple-testing correction [FDR < 0.05]) in ATACseq peaks in CPT-treated WT cDC2. Irf4-/- cDC2 had only one significant ATACseq peak (in the Rasl11a gene); re-expression of IRF4 caused changes in 9 ATACseq regions. These results suggest that cDC2 plasticity is not accompanied by gross changes in chromatin structure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ATACseq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: cAMP regulation of genes in cDC2 may be mediated by alterations in IRF4 expression.
source: By contrast, the presence of an IRF4 binding site was predictive of both up- and down- regulation by CPT (p=3.6×10−5 and 2.6 × 10−6, respectively), implying that cAMP regulation of genes in cDC2 may be mediated by alterations in IRF4 expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ChIPseq and RNAseq data analysis.

claim: CREB1 is a cofactor for IRF4-regulated genes.
source: Unexpectedly, CREB1 was also the major TF 'driver' of genes altered in Irf4-/- cells and Dox-treated Irf4i cells (592 and 442 such genes, 24% and 32%, z-scores 233 and 240, respectively) (Supplementary file 1: containing Supplementary Tables 5-6). These observations implicate CREB1 as a cofactor for IFR4-regulated genes and suggest a link between cAMP signaling and IRF4-regulated transcription in DCs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the transcriptional network analysis.

claim: There is a link between cAMP signaling and IRF4-regulated transcription in DCs.
source: Unexpectedly, CREB1 was also the major TF 'driver' of genes altered in Irf4-/- cells and Dox-treated Irf4i cells (592 and 442 such genes, 24% and 32%, z-scores 233 and 240, respectively) (Supplementary file 1: containing Supplementary Tables 5-6). These observations implicate CREB1 as a cofactor for IFR4-regulated genes and suggest a link between cAMP signaling and IRF4-regulated transcription in DCs.

claim: Endogenous IRF4 is a transcriptional repressor of a subset of cAMP-dependent genes in cDC2s.
source: Further, our data indicate that endogenous IRF4 is a transcriptional repressor of a subset of cAMP-dependent genes in cDC2s, based on the following: 1) its loss causes up-regulation of cAMP-dependent gene expression, 2) presence of an IRF4 binding site is highly predictive of a gene that is regulated by cAMP, and 3) an IRF4 binding site predicts that a gene increases in Irf4-/- cDC2s and decreases in IRF4 restored cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: IRF4 is a major repressor of cAMP-stimulated gene expression in cDCs.
source: We therefore conclude that IRF4 is a major repressor of cAMP-stimulated gene expression in cDCs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the genomic analysis.

claim: A portion of cAMP-stimulated genes in cDCs appear to be indirectly regulated via suppression of Irf4 expression.
source: Thus, a portion of cAMP-stimulated genes in cDCs appear to be indirectly regulated via suppression of Irf4 expression.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: cDC2 cells appear to include two subpopulations: cDC17 (CD11c+, CD11b+, IRF4- or IRF4low, IRF5+), and cDC2 (CD11c+, CD11b+, IRF4+, KLF4+).
source: We propose that cDC2 cells appear to include two subpopulations: cDC17 (CD11c+, CD11b+, IRF4- or IRF4low, IRF5+), and cDC2 (CD11c+, CD11b+, IRF4+, KLF4+).
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the experimental findings.

claim: The PRR-mediated and cAMP-mediated activation pathways converge on CREB to provide phenotypic plasticity of DCs.
source: Overall, these data indicate that curdlan acts via its PRR to induce a Th17 bias by cDC2s by a CREB-dependent, cAMP-PKA-independent pathway. Furthermore, the PRR-mediated and cAMP-mediated activation pathways converge on CREB to provide phenotypic plasticity of DCs, thus defining a new basis for classification of novel cDC2 and cDC17 subsets.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Inhibition of the pro-Th2 DC cDC2 phenotype by cAMP agonists promotes induction of the pro-Th17 DC cDC17 phenotype.
source: Our results thus indicate that: 1) inhibition of the pro-Th2 DC cDC2 phenotype by cAMP agonists promotes induction of the pro-Th17 DC cDC17 phenotype, and 2) reduction of IRF4 levels is necessary but not sufficient for induction of the pro-Th17 transcriptional program in DCs by both the PRR-dependent and cAMP-dependent signaling pathways and by cAMP, also requires IRF5.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Reduction of IRF4 levels is necessary but not sufficient for induction of the pro-Th17 transcriptional program in DCs by both the PRR-dependent and cAMP-dependent signaling pathways.
source: Our results thus indicate that: 1) inhibition of the pro-Th2 DC cDC2 phenotype by cAMP agonists promotes induction of the pro-Th17 DC cDC17 phenotype, and 2) reduction of IRF4 levels is necessary but not sufficient for induction of the pro-Th17 transcriptional program in DCs by both the PRR-dependent and cAMP-dependent signaling pathways and by cAMP, also requires IRF5.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Induction of the pro-Th17 transcriptional program in DCs by cAMP also requires IRF5.
